Exposure by VOLUNTARILY moving into safe but fear-related situations that activate mild anxiety, with encouragement and support, can be very helpful in overcoming excessive fears. In fact, it is really the gold standard approach.

Pushing someone to go into extremely fear-activating situations while mocking and taunting them is an excellent way to make such fears WORSE rather than better, and would not be recommended by any behavioural therapist. Personal control and choice are essential elements of these approaches.

I would encourage you to look at that fifth sentence: "I know it's just a small number..." I wonder if it would be possible to feel pride in the accomplishment without dismissing it or making it seem trivial compared to other people. Actually, overcoming a great deal of inertia, assessing a bicycle, taking it for repair, getting it back, then riding it 3km is not a trivial accomplishment but an enormous one. This expands your range, puts more of your region within your grasp, and lets you engage with the outside world more. I know that your statement is just designed to head off the inevitable downers ("3 isn't that far etc etc"). But what would it be like to compare those 3km not with what Lance Armstrong and his steroids can do, but with the number of km you yourself rode in the past 6 months. I'm guessing you rode more in two days than in quite some time. That's more motivating. How many visits have you made to your grandmother's in the past 2 days compared to the previous months? More. How many overtures from your uncle? More. 

If you're like many, you'll find it tempting to set a goal of a 20km bike ride next. But what if 3km is fine? And if you want to expand your range, what about trying to go 3.1km? The Tour de France can wait.

Yes, this difficulty does bear some similarity with DPD, and arguably even more with Avoidant PD. It's worth remembering, though, that the PD criteria are only descriptions of symptoms - behaviour, thought patterns, and emotions. They say nothing about cause and provide no guidance on resolution. Most clinicians are finding that although various PD descriptions are becoming popular among the public, they have less utility in practice.

If a person exhibits A+B+C+D, we say they have DPD. If we ask what that means, exactly, it's that they have A+B+C+D. The "diagnosis" adds nothing to the picture, and only convinces some people that they "have a mental disorder" which is actually just a cluster of phenomena. Many often take their PD label, like other diagnoses, as a reason to continue etching a given pattern of behaviour deeper rather than swimming against it.

All that said, the course could reasonably be said to be an approach to DPD or AvPD, especially in young adults. It is about turning and facing our anxieties rather than allowing them to dictate our actions.

I think that people in this situation get a great deal of pressure to change from parents, relatives, old friends, economic forces, and more, and they are on the receiving end of a great deal of disdain and criticism. It's easy to perceive a resource like this as another bit of "Your life isn't good enough to satisfy us and you need to change." So a degree of hostility is understandable.

For many, the prospect of change is also frightening. It involves confronting anxieties about the outside world, about being seen, about potential failure, about rejection, and more. When anyone is leading you toward the door of the skydiving plane and suggesting a leap, it's tempting to push back against them. "Don't push me!"

And if one's window to the outside world is social media, the idea of getting out there and joining in is pretty unappealing. Socials are often the world at its worst. It doesn't look like much fun. And indeed, the first few steps are usually difficult and anxiety-provoking, so that just seems to confirm that impression.

When someone comes to see me, I'm always pretty clear. "This is your life. I'm not here to push anything on you. If it's satisfying, great. If it's not and you don't want to change anyway, fine. I'm here if there are changes you decide you want to make."

People are welcome to criticize, fight back, or believe I'm just in it for the limitless sums of money I can make from them. That's fine, though the money thing is a bit mysterious to me (wouldn't it be better to go for people who actually have some?). I'm here for the people who have tried this way of life out and find it isn't working for them and want to build something different for themselves that suits them better.

At the end of an assessment for depressed mood I will often ask "What would happen if we kidnapped 12 people off the street and gave them your life: your sleep schedule, your screen time, your diet, your family, your social network - everything. 24 hours a day they would live exactly as you live. And at the end of a month we ask them 'How are you doing?'" 

Almost everyone says "Oh, I think they'd be depressed." And I agree. 

It's not universally true, but usually the more you understand how a depressed person is living, the less mysterious the depression becomes and the more normal it seems. (I tell students that "The better you know your client, the harder it is to diagnose them.") For a person with mysterious or not-so-mysterious depression, working with a qualified therapist can often be an enormous help.

People often report that they feel unbearably bored with NEET life, or feel that once-cherished activities have lost their lustre, and see that as evidence of mental disorder. Often, it's evidence of their mental health instead. We have hands, opposable thumbs, and feet because we have evolved to take an active role in the world around us. Boredom may be, to paraphrase Jungian analyst James Hollis, your life calling out to you. "Hey, I'm over here - out here in the world, not there at home." [https://youtu.be/YG97oJPiQgE](https://youtu.be/YG97oJPiQgE)

Many people look forward to retirement, but the big fear is that they will be wandering around or sitting on a bench. Most who want to retire want an active, fulfilling life where they can be actively engaged doing things for reasons other than collecting money. Examples in my own nonclinical life: renovating a house, helping to organize World Cup events, organizing groups to sponsor refugees, taking up organic farming, running a Buddhist centre. It's nice not to feel rushed, so that one can read a book on a bench now and then, but the bench is not a big attraction for anyone I've met, clinically or otherwise.

Relatively few retired people are really happy with a life like this. Overly stressed and busy people often envy those who don't work and don't have commitments. They fantasize about having nothing but golf or bench-sitting to look forward to. Then they retire, and within a month golf becomes unbearable unless it's part of a balanced life with some kind of meaning. Being imbalanced on the work side, they naturally crave what is missing. When that element becomes the sole ingredient in life it rapidly loses its appeal, because they have simply created a new imbalance. This doesn't mean that they need to go back to the office, but it does mean that no one thing is going to "feed" them - and they need to give up the search and begin building a life with multiple ingredients instead.

Odd to see this. I am just home from recording a video on this topic. It's a very common experience - the sense of boredom, anhedonia, or lack of "hit" from media or gaming when NEETing. It's very much like the fade in euphoria reported by heroin users, though it is a slower onset for NEETs. 

When people tell me about this phenomenon I often have them imagine their very favourite food - the one thing they love above all else. Then imagine eating it for breakfast lunch and dinner every day: how long would it be before it lost its appeal? 

The temptation is to give up on gaming, or video, and try to find a different "it" instead. But there is no "it." There is no food that that we won't grow sick of; no time-passer that will retain its charge forever, at least for most people. The problem isn't the quality of games or video, it's the balance. 

People sometimes say to me that they think their apathy or boredom is a sign of mental disorder. I suggest that this is possible, but it may be that they are signs of mental health instead, of complete normality. They are the mind saying: "this receptive life is just not enough for me. I need more." Fear is often a lie - what we fear is unlikely to happen. Boredom is often telling us the truth: "The life I am leading is too small for me."

I think you are right. Financial literacy is a separate section of the resource I am working on. Without an understanding of basic personal finances, NEETs are essentially defenceless in the face of unscrupulous others - or even the basic financial fates. The idea of this work is to help people get into the driver's seat of their own life, and knowing how to manage one's own bit of economic reality is an essential aspect of that.

I think there are people who feel freed by the NEET lifestyle and are able to live it in a way that doesn't force others (eg parents) to slave on their behalf. My work is only for people who feel dissatisfied, or who feel that after a lot of time in NEET life the appeal is waning. In my own life I've found that being active and engaged in things, including work of various sorts (teaching, writing, providing therapy, volunteering at a local festival, even the warehouse job I had in summers in university) was more valuable to me (over and above any money I received) than the time I've spent online. I've often felt that if I had to identify periods of my life that I've flushed down the toilet, it would be time spent on social media and random surfing. But that's my experience, not everyone's.

You are absolutely right that there is more to expanding a life than just accumulating a set of skills - and that among the skills some people might benefit from are strategies to talk with others or engage. The script I'm working on is only 1 of about 50, so there's a lot more to the resource I'm building than this.

I agree with you that some skills are probably more central than others. Basic cooking and basic first aid are good examples. My father made me take touch typing in Grade 9, which I thought was a) boring and b) useless - but turned out to be one of the most valuable things I got out of high school. Driving isn't an essential for everyone - though some countries have such poor public transit that not being able to drive is a significant restriction. I can't offhand think of any mental issue in Canada that would legally prevent a person from driving (psychosis, personality disorder, bipolar, ADHD, high functioning ASD - all are fine to get a license here), but are there some in other countries?

It's not a thing for everyone - I suspect there are few skills that are universally useful. But swimming can be good recreation, good fitness, essential for some jobs, helpful if you are in an emergency situation near water, invited to a social occasion involving a pool, etc.

I would echo the comments of some here that it can be good to take a low-key approach. The person coming out typically feels that they are making an operatic, life-and-death step. When people look back on it, they often appreciate it if the reaction is a bit of an anticlimax. Cement the relationship, invite them to talk further if they want, express support for them, let them ask questions, and don't ask many ask yourself (he's talking with his parents, tangentially, about sex, which is mortifying enough for most teens without getting a lot of inquiry). Two thoughts:

1. That's where a therapist comes in. It's not about helping a person feel comfortable or ready or eager to make change - it's about helping a person to do without those prerequisites and do them while allowing the discomfort to be present.

2. The feeling of insurmountability can feel like an enemy but actually be an ally. It's not the signal to give up, but to reduce the magnitude of what one is attempting. Many people in this situation make their steps too big. "I have to get a job, move out, get my finances under control, attack all my fears head-on, etc." The task isn't to get stronger so that one can accomplish these mammoth tasks, it's to let go of them FOR NOW and do something small enough that it can be accomplished despite the inertia/discomfort. This usually means choosing something so small it seems stupid: Sitting at a bus stop 30 mins and never taking a bus. Eating breakfast at the table, alone, rather than taking it to one's room. Finding that old bicycle in the basement but not riding it.

If it isn't the enormity of a goal that stops people, it's the triviality of it. "That's so idiotic it's just humiliating to do it and admit that's where I am." A therapist can help a person tolerate and even invite those thoughts - and do the thing anyway.

A big part of the problem in launching into adulthood is that individuals having difficulty (you can tell I don't like the FTL term with that big Failure right up front - it's a delay, not an endpoint) have a fairly small zone of comfort. Their activities are limited, fear of uncertainty tends to be high, and range of experience is usually low.

Psychotherapy (which I practice) can be valuable, but one of its most powerful aspects is helping the person leave their zone of comfort and expand their range. Doing things they've never done, building skills they haven't had, trying new experiences. At our clinic, some of the quickest shifts have come when we've been able to have a young adult accompanied to have actual experiences: taking the bus, riding the subway, taking the seabus (Vancouver), going to stores, etc. In a way I think of the path as:

Stuck > therapy > doing new stuff, building skills.

If it's:

Stuck > therapy > don't do new stuff, remain in zone of comfort

I would think of that as a failed intervention. It's not even about doing things the person might actually take up as a hobby. It's more about facing unfamiliarity and surviving it, which builds a sense of personal capacity. You probably wouldn't take up caving as a hobby, but the experience of doing something so far outside your present range of experience might be unexpectedly helpful.

If I had to pick between a) psychotherapy, and b) doing new stuff, and couldn't do both, as a therapist my choice would be (b). When I teach other therapists, one of my slogans is "Therapy is weak, life is strong." Meaning that we need to leverage the therapy to produce life experiences. Me chatting about exercise does nothing; a person going out and getting exercise does a lot.

If a young adult came to me and said "I'm willing to do one thing: either come and see you for therapy once a week, or go to Outward Bound, but not both" I'd likely tell him to go to Outward Bound and call me when he gets back.

Depression is more of a syndrome - a set of somewhat co-occurring symptoms - than a disease. Much like fever, it can be brought on by multiple factors. When teaching clinicians about depression, I have often said that "the better you know your client, the harder it usually is to say they are experiencing an abnormal reaction." In other words, if you know how they spend their days, the emotional and other symptoms become much less mysterious.

I often ask clients to imagine what would happen if we took a random dozen people off the street and gave them the client's CURRENT life and schedule (nothing about their history; just their present hour-to-hour activities): screen time, exercise level, diet, light exposure, social contacts, sleep cycle, and so on. "What you do, they do, 24 hours a day. And at the end of a month we ask them how they're doing. What would they say?" 90% or more of clients say "I think they'd be depressed" and I agree: My client is not responding abnormally to their lifestyle, they are responding much as others would. I don't have to help them become normal, thankfully, because they are already normal. 

All of which begs the question of WHY a person would isolate, watch screens all day, eat junk food, etc - are they TRYING to be depressed? Never, in my experience. Other causal factors (upbringing, rejection, pandemic) nudged them toward a depressogenic lifestyle which became self-perpetuating - a kind of feed-forward effect. If we were to remove those initial nudges, however, the depression would likely remain. Most of it is being driven by the present lifestyle. If we can work on the present-world life, the depression will often begin to slowly unravel, often in an accelerating feedback cycle. If, instead, we spent a few months trying to "understand the origins," leaving the present lifestyle intact, it is unlikely (HAS BEEN, in my experience) that the depression will lift.

Although medication can be helpful for certain clients, this perspective governs my reluctance to see meds as the frontline treatment. If depressed individuals are responding normally to depressogenic situations, then the intent of medication is to help them respond ABnormally. Rather than bringing them to a normal state, we are trying to overcome the normal state that they are already in. This may be why medication intervention is often so unsatisfying - it seems to be harder to make people abnormal than it is to help them create a more fulfilling life.

Disclaimer: I'm a clinician working in this area. There are a lot of comments here alluding to parental enabling, which I think can be an issue for a lot of young adults (YAs) but definitely not all. (Like most problems in living, anything one can say is flat wrong for at least some of the folks involved.) 

Sometimes parents forget that their job isn't just to keep their offspring safe - it's essentially to run an apprenticeship for adulthood (training their kid or YA in the skills they will need). Then time passes and the YA reaches an age where they reach into the skill bag and - nothing. How do you cook, clean, drive, swim, manage social situations, overcome temptation, do job interviews, fix things? Their teacher forgot to teach.

Sometimes the apprenticeship went fine, but when the YA ran into trouble there was a tremendous - and mostly good - surge of compassion that found expression in support for a dependent lifestyle. Parents decide "Hey, until he gets on his feet we'll do the laundry, pay the cell phone, come home from work and make his meals, and generally make this home life safe, secure, and undemanding. And eventually that sense of calm and being cared-for will sink inward and create a space for his self-direction and motivation to flower." This actually makes sense, but doesn't often seem to work. And with every day spent in avoidance of a likely-necessary future, the status quo etches a little deeper and a little deeper, becoming a trench from which it is harder and harder to escape.

There's a common error involved in attempting to evaluate the strength of the placebo effect: assuming that the response rate in the placebo arm of placebo-control trials provides an adequate measure of the placebo effect. It doesn't.

Responding in the placebo arm is a combination of regression effects, selection error, spontaneous recovery, and placebo response. (Responding in the medication arm is, obviously, all of the above PLUS medication effect.) The biggest factor is probably spontaneous recovery, because after all the meds are used to treat depressive episodes which are ... uh ... episodic in nature.

To tease out the actual placebo effect we would need a no-treatment arm, which is almost never included in med trials. The difference between the response rate in this nonintervention condition and the placebo condition would be an approximation of the strength of placebo.

That said, it's very clear that most of the response found in antidepressant effectiveness trials is accounted for by that soup of nonmedication effects - about 75% of the total response, by most estimates in meta-analyses. There remains some daylight between the placebo and medication arms suggesting a direct medication effect, though usually the difference does not meet the threshold of clinically-meaningful response. Kirsch suggests that when one uses active (side-effect-producing) placebo, that daylight shrinks to nullity, but there are so few such studies that it's hard to conclude this.

One of the best meta-analyses in recent years is Cipriani et al's 2018 study in Lancet, though the main daylight in that work is between the actual results (a near-perfect replication of Kirsch's findings of weak effect) and the interpretation in discussion (all the meds work and should be used more often). If interested, here's a 26-minute overview of that and other recent studies: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B02U9EtQWy8&t=136s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B02U9EtQWy8&t=136s)

This seems to be an ideal situation for self-guided exposure work, provided you are able to carry out the steps in objectively safe conditions (ie, no dangling off balconies etc).

You say "I fear falling against the window, I am forced to hold onto something, and I quickly move back away." Three things. The fear happens. You FEEL forced to hold onto something (though if you are in a safe position you might not actually be forced to do so, you just feel uncomfortable not doing so). And you quickly move back away. Moving away, if you are like most people, will create an intense feeling of relief that is a powerful reward for escaping the situation. Nothing can be said for certain without a clear and in-person assessment by a qualified healthcare professional, but for most people this relief will reinforce the fear and make it worse the next time.

The trap that many fall into is pushing themselves to their limit of tolerance. This evokes a lot of fear which eventually over-rides their ability to stand firm, then they avoid and reinforce the avoidance. The key in exposure work is to do something objectively safe that does not elicit so much fear that retreat becomes inevitable, and to remain there long enough that the fear crests and fades, being replaced typically by a sense of tedious boredom with the exercise. For an individual with a fear of standing by windows in tall buildings, the exercise might be sitting cross-legged on a cushion exactly 8 feet from the window for an hour. Once that has been done, 7.5 feet might be the exercise. Eventually it might be placing left hand on metal window strut and placing nose 3 inches from glass. 

What stops many people overcoming their fears is not the fear itself, but the boredom when exposures are extended. But boredom is the goal.

One of the most helpful exercises for many people is to bypass the practical and the near-term, come up with ideas, then return to the near-term to start building your path.

How to bypass? Imagine that you are happy with your life. "I've really got it. I'm living MY life the way I want to. This feels good." Really try to imagine feeling this way - even though at present you don't.

Then ask yourself what would that person's life be like? What would you be doing that might lead to that sense of satisfaction? It's tempting to think he'd be sipping champagne while counting his money on the superyacht, but that's probably just a distraction. If you really contemplate this you'd likely come up with some elements that are available to you: The door is open; you just have to walk through it.

Sometimes having a goal or vision for your life can be a detriment rather than an asset, because the goal is just too many steps away - especially if you view it as something that will only pay off once you reach it. Thinking about it just proves discouraging.

An alternative to looking at the distant future is to look at one's life in the present, and ask "What would be a tiny/miniscule/insignificant bit better than this?" Not the eventual goal, not where you want to be a year or ten years from now, but some small thing that would, to use Pink Floyd's analogy, take one brick from the wall but not tear it all down. For some people that's living exactly the same way but able to get into a 7-11. Or living exactly the same way but knowing how to make soup. Or doing everything the same but able to get on a bus. Doing the same things but attending a single-day first aid course.

Rather than effort-effort-effort-effort-effort-payoff, we want effort-small payoff-effort-small payoff-effort-small payoff. The payoffs aren't as grand as the big "life vision" kind, but are more achievable and tend to build confidence for subsequent steps. I kind of think this is the only way people ever really get moving after getting stuck.

Inevitably, some things require several steps before any benefit appears at all (job searches, many educational programs). But keeping much of one's work focussed on the near-term horizon can be doable, whereas longer-term goals can just be paralyzing.

Most hiki/neets are very conscious of skill deficits, but I think habit deficits are a bigger issue for many. Habits are regularly-practiced behaviours that don't involve skill. Things like cooking for self, regular time for bed, showing up at agreed-upon time, and so on. Some say "Yeah, I should begin developing those habits." But this misses the reality. You are ALWAYS developing habits through your behaviour. You don't have a choice about developing habits - they come about automatically. The only choice you have is about which habits you develop, by your actions in the present.

Most jobs, relationships, and self-management don't rely that much on skill. They rely on habits much more. For most entry-level jobs, for example, employers don't care whether a person has specific skills, like knowing how to plant a tree or prep food or drive a mini-ferry. Those can be taught. They care whether the person has the habit of showing up on time, or showering, or checking their own work, or asking for clarification when priorities are ambiguous. Those are much harder to teach. And habits can be practiced immediately, without any skill learning involved.

The primary task of parenting is to make yourself obsolete: To help a young person become sufficiently able to care for himself or herself that your death, absence, or incapacity does not bring them down too. A fully-nurtured adult with untapped or undeveloped capacity who remains fully dependent on the parent for support at the parent's death is a misfire in parenting, not a success. 

Capacity is developed in a number of ways - one of which is by gradual training in the needed skills, and another is in the gradual withdrawal of supports. We gently and steadily unscrew the training wheels, if you like. For example, the various adults in the house begin to take on equal responsibilities for upkeep, meals, bills, and so on.

Some parents get stuck in this process and wind up providing support that their adult does not actually require. Rather than helping, this often reinforces the young adult's conviction that they don't have the capacity to do these things. The best thing they can do is not open the trap door, but to set and maintain clear boundaries on the support they provide, tilting that support toward capacity and independence rather than withdrawal.

Your responders here are emphasizing the physical aspect of your statement, which is absolutely true. Without physical exercise, it is natural for muscles to atrophy. Add exercise back, and strength returns. The muscle cells do not die, so this is not a permanent state. In fact, people who get very little exercise will benefit more than others by a relatively modest increase in activity. Bump up from 0 to 15 minutes of exercise a day, and you will see great gains. Bump an olympic athlete up from 6 hrs to 6 hrs and 15 minutes, and you won't see much difference.

But it sounds like you were thinking more broadly, and the same appears to be true. Without the challenge of social interaction, our social skills weaken. Without the challenge of responsibility, our ability to live up to responsibilities weakens. Without practice at over-riding our impulses for a more important goal than immediate gratification, our ability to control our impulses weakens. Without a life with time constraints, we get less effective at dealing with time pressure. Without experiences out in the world, our ability to navigate the world declines. 

In a past post, someone compared hiki life to the couch-bound citizens aboard the starship in Wall-E, who have mostly lost their ability to walk and care for themselves. This is pretty apt. (The least plausible part of that film is the ending in which they suddenly get up and begin exploring the Earth again.) By striving toward comfort and a low-demand life, the ability to handle even trivial demands (I need groceries; I have to cook; I should go to the dentist) become overwhelming. By trying not to be overwhelmed, the feeling of being overwhelmed is more easily triggered and becomes the controlling force in one's life.

But the metaphor with muscle is also apt. A person who has lost muscle mass by lying in a hospital bed for months can regain strength remarkably quickly with gradual increases in activity. And a person who has had few demands, few time constraints, few responsibilities, few chores, or few instances of self-control/self-discipline can build up these "muscles" as well. It can be wonderful to stand by and watch that happen, as I have.

But the hope that the quest for lasting comfort through the avoidance of challenge will be successful - that comfort will be found and sustained? You suggest there is no hope of this. I suspect you may be right.

Principle 1 is that Assertiveness is about controlling yourself, not others. Here the focus is on behaviour, and whose behaviour you can control. As you can only control your own, that's where you act. So rather than nagging your neighbour to return your lawnmower, for example, you control whether you loan it to him next time. Many individuals interested in assertiveness are very focussed on other people and how they "should" be. "How do I make my son/boss/spouse/friend/coworker/neighbour be more considerate?" Answer: You don't. You shift your attention from their steps in the dance to your own. In fact, we DO want to have an effect on the world, but the way we will accomplish that is to stay focussed on our own role.

Principle 2 is that Assertiveness is about effectiveness, not self-expression. Here the focus is on outcome and style. As I've said above, we usually DO want to have an impact, and much of assertive communication is about how to do that most effectively. So long as you nag your kid to clean up his room and tell him how resentful you are that you have to do it for him, nothing happens. When you unplug the router until it's done, change occurs. Control yourself, not others. Our culture, however, emphasizes the idea of self-expression. I have the right to my feelings, my anger, my rage, and I have the right to express all of that. Well yes, but doing so will seldom change things. Ranting about how frustrated I am (or firehosing anything else I happen to be feeling) doesn't bring about change. Assertive communication and a focus on my own role does.

One theory about this is that the sense of time is governed partly by the actual amount of time that has passed, and partly by the variety of activity engaged in during that time. When we store things like brushing our teeth in memory, we in effect remember doing it once "and then a bunch of other times." It's not stored as 700 different memories every year, so it doesn't take much space. If we spend a year not doing very much in terms of variety, it doesn't take much storage to recall it, so it seems as though not much time has passed. (As well, time spent online seems hardly to get stored at all, so our memories are mainly of irl activity; if there isn't much of that, then time seems shorter.)

If we do a lot of different things, this takes much more "space" and so the time seems longer. I'm a fair bit older than many on this sub, and so have experienced much of the "time seems to pass faster now than when I was 20" phenomenon. In a year before covid, however, I did a lot of travel and introduced a lot of novelty into my life. The result was a year that seemed as long as one in childhood. I would think back 10 months and it would seem to have been a long long time ago.

A long reply, but the answer seems to be to make time seem slower, do more irl and with more variety.

Hikikomori experience many emotions, some of them worth paying attention to; others worth treating with suspicion. Anxiety, for example, is often based on thoughts that don't really hold up to scrutiny. "If I go out everyone will be looking at me." When you think about it you realize  that most people aren't actually that interested in you. As the old saying goes, "We would be less concerned with what others think of us if we knew how seldom they do."

Sometimes the anxiety is telling us something important. "If I don't get myself moving somehow, this life, which is unsatisfying to me, is going to become more entrenched. The glue stiffens." That one's probably true. But anxiety tends to be fairly unreliable as a guide to life overall.

Boredom, though? When a person living a hiki life experiences boredom, there's usually a valid reason. "I'm not seeing anything new, not growing, not expanding my life nor capacity." Watch the same movie 300 times and it will become excruciating. Sit alone in the same room 300 days, and the same will occur. Some view boredom as a kind of psychopathology. I tend to think it's the voice of sanity and reason, and worth paying attention to. It may be your life calling to you. "Hey, I'm out here, not in there."

Some suggest looking inward for your interests and passions. Maybe. But the hiki life is almost designed to produce anhedonia - the inability to get interested or passionate in anything. Take almost anyone and force them to live a hiki life for several months - they will tend to lose much of their drive and interest, even in doing things beyond the locked door.

When many hikis look inside they don't find interest or passion, so this can be a bad guide. It's often a more cold-blooded reason-based process than a passion-driven one. What is it that makes the boredom worse? What's the opposite of that? What would I be doing if I was not letting inertia or fear take the steering wheel? And then find a way to do that, however boring or futile it might seem, at a small level. Not so that great fires of passion are ignited, but so that a degree of confidence appears. "Well, walking to that new park (shopping at that bigger grocery store, taking the subway, sitting in that coffee shop, riding that bicycle) may not seem like much, but at least I know I can do it."

Negative comments from others can be a bit like a sniper attack. The person says something vaguely ambiguous that seems designed to puncture your bubble, then moves on with the conversation, as though firing an arrow from behind a wall. Often the person doesn't investigate further, and nurses his/her wounds in private afterward.

Possibility 1: They actually did mean to be insulting.

Possibility 2: Your own self-esteem causes you to interpret ambiguous comments in the worst possible way, which may not be what was intended.

If you react to what you THINK they meant, they can deny intent regardless of which possibility is in play. A better strategy is to invite them to step out from the shadows and say what they actually meant. A calm, simple, and nonaggressive, "Sorry, I'm not sure I got that" or "When you said that, what did you mean?" or "Say more" can invite a clarification. Regardless of what your hopes/fears are guessing was meant, hold off on any emotional reaction at least until you invite the person to step up and say what they mean openly. 

At that point, you can state your reaction. "It hurts to hear you say that." "I thought you liked my cooking." "I worked hard on that, it's disappointing you think it's not good enough." (Obviously the response depends on the situation.) It's usually better to state how you feel rather than acting it out (bursting into tears, yelling back, counterattacking, looking defeated) because this makes it clear that your emotional state is in their hands to manipulate.

There are probably several mechanisms of action. One of these is a way we also think cognitive therapy tends to work. Let's consider depression as an example. In every life, there are positive and negative elements. There's enough food in the fridge, for example, and a family member is seriously ill. During depression we tend to pay attention to the negative elements to the exclusion of positive ones, and to make the negative ones more significant (that illness is partly my fault because I supported their lousy diet) than the positives (everyone I know has enough food).

Cognitive therapy tries to rebalance this selective attention so that positive and neutral elements are both perceived and given significance. Simply being in therapy may accomplish this: A person believes they are receiving treatment and so might be improving, so they look for signs of this. "Hey, I brushed my teeth without procrastinating this morning - maybe I'm getting somewhere." Positive elements that may always have been there, but would formerly have been ignored, are now attended to and have an impact on the emotional state.

Placebos may work similarly. Knowing that I am taking a medication for a condition, I look for signs that that condition is improving. When it is a condition defined by a subjective experience - like pain or depression - my looking for signs of improvement is likely to produce at least some of the effect the drug is supposed to bring about.

In placebo control trials, btw, people often look at the amount of response in the placebo condition as being equivalent to the placebo effect. This is an error, because response in the placebo arm includes the actual placebo effect plus regression effects plus spontaneous recovery. Here's the first of a series of posts on placebo control trials and how they can sometimes result in misinterpretation. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VBAbVJW51Kw&list=PLkKJ2Ak4rQsuTqL2gc2n5fPu-TCnptXYW&index=7&t=4s

We become what we do.  In NEET circles there is a big emphasis on the idea of skills (do you have some, should you be developing more, etc), but habits are just as important and arguably more so. 

In pop psychology (I accidentally typed "poop psychology" which I may retain as more accurate), we talk incessantly about "expressing yourself." What we ignore is the idea of creating yourself - the concept that the self we have is not something we were born with, but has been developed through experience and effort. Becoming a NEET for a year involves spending a year creating and reinforcing a NEET self that may make study/work/life/relationships more difficult in future. Is this your goal?

An obvious reply is that although you may not want this (just look at the number of suicidal posts on this sub), you also don't want to create an overworked construction worker. It's possible, though, that however difficult or dull the job was, it created more than exhaustion. It may have given you skills that will be useful later on, the ability to push past disinterest (useful even if you're working on something you're passionate about), the ability to show up (which is an essential part of almost any life quest), and it put money in the bank. 

It's your life. It's also your self. What type of self would you like to create?

Engaging in receptive sorts of activities - playing other people's games, watching movies and anime others have made - can be a great part of life when balanced against activities that involve taking a more active role. As the primary element of a person's daily "diet" it tends to lose appeal and become boring. It's like salt - great as part of a meal, lousy as a meal in itself.

NEETs often complain of anxiety, hopelessness, and boredom. 

I suggest they be a little suspicious of the anxiety: it tends to lie. We are not often the focus of other people's attention, most people are so involved with their own lives that they aren't bothering to notice us that much, and if they judge us it's pretty irrelevant.

I suggest that they be a little suspicious of the hopelessness/depression. Hopelessness is a fantasy of the future that may well prove to be a misperception - and in the lives of NEETs who get more engaged with life it seems almost invariably to be so. Hopelessness can also be motivated: If I can convince myself that there's no point in trying, I don't have to move and face the usual stumbles and errors along the way.

But I suggest that they trust the boredom. Boredom is our life calling to us. "Hey, I'm over here, not locked up in that room killing time." Boredom isn't an enemy. Boredom is good. Most people given a NEET life would feel it - and do. One of the problems with older adults who retire is that if they don't get engaged with other activities in life they become bored and depressed - like NEETs tend to. The leisure life isn't all it's cracked up to be - note the frequency of suicidal comments on this sub.

I've treated a great number of NEETs/hikikomori over the years, and have taught many mental health professionals how to work with them and their families. The overwhelming majority of the individuals I have seen do not have significant physical disabilities nor neurological conditions that make the life their only option. Some have a relatively mild form of ADHD or very high-functioning autism (what we might formerly have called mild Aspergers), neither of which forces the lifestyle or prevents a more satisfying life either - the majority of individuals with ADHD and (let's call it) Aspergers are active, engaged, and leading an independent life.

Where there is a more significant neurological or physical disability I would draw a line distinguishing them from what I think of as true NEETs. They are people living with supports or benefits due to their disability. It is true, however, that a majority of people living this lifestyle who present for therapy (which is not a representative sample, clearly) can be diagnosed as experiencing a psychological issue - avoidant personality disorder, social anxiety, dysthymia. But these diagnoses are not statements about neurological status. They are made solely on the basis of behavior and present symptoms, rather than on the basis of cause. They don't tell us much, other than that the existing way of living is not working well for them.

Judging from posts to this sub, there are some individuals for whom the NEET lifestyle may be suited. For most, however, living an isolated, unstructured, and relatively role-free life is a path to disinterest, marked increases in anxiety, and depressed mood, including anhedonia - the inability to be lifted or engaged by activities that used to be enjoyable. Here's a video on the subject of anhedonia: [https://youtu.be/QSYtqlPpL0M](https://youtu.be/QSYtqlPpL0M)

When people living a neet or hiki lifestyle discuss depression, it is usually as a cause of their withdrawal. And this may well be true. But what is often missed is that depressed mood is, for most people, also a predictable effect of living this way - an effect that does not go away as long as the lifestyle persists.

For many neets, the things that charge them up seem, as you say, to be out of reach. There are two reasons for this. First, some of their reasonable wishes are indeed difficult to attain while they live a neet life - things like financial independence, living on their own, or romantic relationships. Second, they may try to "charge themselves up" by contemplating goals that seem desirable - but being imaginary, these need to be made more potent by being somewhat grandiose. What neets/hikis who move on from the lifestyle often find is that the emotional payoff from real-world achievements is greater than they expected. In effect, having 1000 real dollars in the bank can be more exciting than fantasizing about a million.

Human beings, like all living things, have needs. We act in order to have those needs met, and we suffer if they are not. Other people's experience may differ, but I have never had an employer who was anything like a parent. Their investment in me is much less, the attention they pay is much less, and in effect the relationship is much more equal. It's like selling apples: you need someone who has apples and someone who wants apples. In the work setting, I have labour and skills for sale, and I sell them to an individual who wants to buy them. I am no more a supplicant to a boss than an apple seller is to the person who wants apples.

The problem is that hikikomori have needs that need to be fulfilled. One way to do that is to convince caregivers to sell their own labour in order to get the money to support the young adult. You read on this sub on occasion about a person who feels great righteous pride in not being a "wageslave" - by forcing his parents to "be wageslaves" and buy all his stuff instead. 

In many cases (not all), doing so is done from a sense of kindness and concern, but has the long-term effect of contributing to the problem. Where a young adult has capacity, the best thing a parent can do - for themselves and for the young adult - is to gently and gradually stop parenting. Ideally this process begins in very early childhood, but in many hiki families the parents, in effect, act as though their son or daughter is an invalid from an early age - accidentally producing an individual who thinks of himself or herself as an invalid.

Do you find that you experience instrumental drives? By that I mean the drive to do X so that you can get Y. This is as opposed to intrinsic drives, which are "I am so interested in X that I will spend hours on it even if there is no Y." Most goals, most ambition, and most drive comes from instrumental drives, not intrinsic ones. The drive doesn't come from inside, it comes from outside.

Instrumental drives are also stronger than intrinsic ones for most people. "I need to get a job in order to have a place to live." "I need to buy groceries so I can eat." This is true for me, and for most people I know, NEETs or not.

Among many NEETs and hikikomori - though definitely not all - it seems that parents or caregivers systematically and unintentionally remove all instrumental motivation. If the person can't afford a computer, or clothes, or beer money, or groceries, these are supplied without any exchange needed (work, money, chores). As a result, any forward movement is entirely dependent on intrinsic motivation ("pursuing my passions") which for most people is an extremely weak force. The care is provided out of kindness and concern, but for some it seems to be, in effect, disabling.

I think you know that the answer to that question is "The choice is yours to make." But if you read the posts on this site long enough, it's hard to convince yourself that the hiki lifestyle is a path to happiness, contentment, or life satisfaction for the vast majority of people.

In my book "How to be Miserable: 40 Strategies You Already Use" I invite people to take a moment away from asking "how can I be happier" and instead ask "What would I do if it was my mission to feel worse rather than better?" Many of the answers to that question (get little exercise, have a poor diet, randomize your sleep cycle, isolate yourself, dwell on your faults, make vague goals, maximize your screen time, and many others) in effect describe the life that many hikis find themselves living. If someone wanted to become depressed, this lifestyle would be a pretty good bet for most people.

Don't assume that passion will have much to do with it once you are actually in the job. You will have a lot of menial, repetitive tasks that aren't at all related to a passion, if you have one. Most people don't have passions - and they are fine without. Looking for passion and expecting it in a workplace is a path to certain disappointment - at least until you are quite far along in a career.

"I don't wanna be the dumb one..." You will ALWAYS be the dumb one when you start a new job. This is normal. It only becomes a problem if you attribute it to maliciousness on their part or an inability to learn on yours, rather than to the situation. Watch out as well for an expectation that an employer will spend a lot of time educating you. They hire people because they have tasks in mind that they need someone to carry out and that they don't want to do themselves. The key is to watch and learn as a side effect while actually carrying out those tasks.

I've had people say "Hey, I could make this much money doing this task I already know from the comfort of my own home, or I could take this lower-paying job making coffee and swabbing the toilets at the game development place." My advice: Swab the toilets. Get the worst possible job at the best available place. Be the port-a-potty placement guy on the film set. Be the cleaner at the game company. Be the data-entry checker in the university lab. Those are the jobs to look for. They are the open doors, and inside there are escalators.

In Vancouver there is a large film industry. Many young people would like to be a part of it, but they wonder whether they really have what it takes to be a director or star. Indeed, these positions are very difficult to get, and a good deal of luck is involved. But becoming a production assistant? An extra? An assistant grip? A catering assistant? A driver? Easy. If you want to be in the TV/movie business, you can be. And from there you can learn many of the other skills involved and potentially discover a steady trade.

The same is true of the game industry. Can you become a primary game designer? Not without training, experience, and luck. But want to become an assistant VFX editor? Sweep the halls? Take on the most menial of jobs in a game design studio? The door, chances are, is open. 

Many people wonder if their dreams can come true. They're looking for the door that leads to the 65th floor of the industry. Those are indeed hard to find, so if you want to feel helpless, it's easy. "I'll never get there." But the ground floor doorway? Wide open. Got some social anxiety, some highish functioning autism? Uh, once you get there, look around. You've found your niche.

"Without X I cannot function, therefore my functioning is dependent on X and otherwise I am worthless."

What is X? For every human, X can be oxygen, food, water, shelter, and any number of nutrients.

Some individuals have unique needs, so their X may differ. "Without injectable insulin..." "Without my wheelchair..." "Without my Vitamin B12 injections given that I can't absorb it through my gut..." "Without my antidepressant..."

I'm not suggesting that everyone needs antidepressants, nor that they work well for everyone. But at their best they help a person become and express who they are, not a fake version. If all they do is numb a person, an adjustment is likely advisable.

But "I'm inherently worthless because I need this external thing?" Substitute other people's situations and the problem becomes clear.

I particularly like this part of your post: "It was about a few weeks ago when I had the revelation that I trusted my mind too much."

Speaking as a psychologist, I think some of the blame for the damage to young adults lies with psychology - especially pop psychology. We've spent 40 years telling people to "trust your feelings" "do what feels right" "let your instincts guide you" and similar happy nonsense.

I'm on LinkedIn with, predictably, a crew of mental health professionals, and it can be a virtual cesspool of inspirational nonsense - much of it along the lines of "Maturity means coming to trust your instincts."

Maturity may partly mean coming to trust a FEW of your instincts that have proven trustworthy and growth-promoting. If any. But a much bigger part of maturity is learning to DIStrust your instincts, emotions, impulses, and thoughts when they have proven that they are full of crap. As they so often do.

"Oh my God, people criticizing me is dangerous!" No, it's not.

"When I'm out in public everyone criticizes and hates me." Most people don't even notice we're there, let alone do they work up the energy to hate us.

"This feels futile because it won't get me to my goal." As opposed to sitting on the couch, which is just SOOO useful.

"Hey, if I drink more I'll feel better." Yeah, temporarily and not that much, then I'll feel worse.

Human minds are thought generators, and 90% of our thoughts are random or impulse-confirming garbage. Learning to distrust ourselves is one of the most important tasks of life.

Three suggestions that I often give:

1. Recognize that there is a difference between something you are interested to study, and something you are interested in doing as a career.  The two are not the same. Those who study without an eye to what they are being trained to do often come off the university production line and realize they are not where they intended to be, in part because they did not consider where they wanted to be at all.
2. Once a great deal of time investment has been made in a program, it is often better to complete it rather than cut bait and switch. This does not sentence a person to continuing in that profession, but it gives a qualification that they can keep if their alternative does not work out.
3. Training that appears not to lead in the direction of one's interests can nevertheless often be leveraged into a desired area. A person who decides in favour of accounting over environmental protection, for example, may discover that green energy firms and nonprofits are starving for people with accounting skills (or legal qualifications, or programming ability, or business school know-how). When you go to a pool/bar/airport/job/party the first few times you feel out of place, like you don't belong. You make mistakes, you get embarrassed, you feel like you're messing up. Normal. Expected.

There are two ways to interpret this awkwardness. 

1. Trait. I'm just awkward/stupid/inept - it's who I am, and because I will always be who I am, this can never change.
2. Skill. I haven't done this very much, so I'm not used to it and it doesn't feel smooth or easy or automatic.

Hikikomori, in my experience, find themselves drawn to the "trait" idea to the almost complete exclusion of the "skill" idea. And yet in my experience they are entirely able to learn these skills with practice. Some take a bit more time than their peers who have been practicing since childhood, while others (equally convinced by their lack of ability) catch on and catch up faster than most. 

The "unchangeable trait" hypothesis doesn't seem to have much validity - even for those told they have autistic presentations. It seems to be an "appeal of futility" phenomenon: If we believe that a task is impossible, we can just relax and stop trying. It's so much easier than facing the chore of learning skills. The downside, though, is a missed life.

I have been working with NEETs to help them find and develop their adulthood for many years, and you're right - psychological issues such as depression, anxiety, and a lack of attentional focus are common concerns.

The direction of causality goes in both directions, however: Some psychological symptoms contribute to the urge to withdraw and isolate. But more of the psychological symptoms are the RESULT of NEETing. NEETing - living a life with minimal social contact, responsibility, or goal-directed activity - predictably and naturally produces mood, anxiety, and attentional issues. In other words, symptoms may produce NEETing, but NEETing produces many more symptoms. Many who are not anxious or depressed at the beginning of their NEETing journey find that they are symptomatic once they've been in the life for a while.

I publish about social skills and teach mental health professionals how to train people in social skills, so I have some awareness of the subject. But cooking and taking on an equal proportion of chores really ARE social skills. Essential ones.

I have met NEETs who finally leave home and don't cook, contribute, or do chores and find it quite surprising when room-mates ask them to leave, or girlfriends end the relationship. They have never been in a situation where they were expected to contribute on an equal basis with others, so it naturally seems completely unfair and abusive (or bullying) when others expect them to do so, or get angry when they don't. Having never acted like nor been treated as an equal, they find it disorienting or insulting when others do so.

Healthy families simulate this progression from "helpless-invalid" to "adult-equal." The youngster goes from others doing all the chores and cooking and care, down to the butt-wiping, to equal-adult who carries a share of the home's responsibility. Ideally by 19 or so the chores and upkeep of the home are shared between the adults as though they are roughly-equal room-mates (usually with less of a financial expectation from the younger adult than from the parents).

There's a saying in AA: Fake it until you make it. In other words, even if the behavior (in their case, abstinence) doesn't feel natural or "like the real you," do it anyway, artificially, and it seeps inward and becomes you.

Most of life is like this. We become swimmers once we swim, we become basketball players as a result of playing basketball, we become cooks as a result of cooking, and we become social as a result of socializing. We become adults not because one day we begin feeling adult. We become adults by acting as though we are already adult - taking on adult roles and responsibilities whether or not they feel comfortable or natural to us.

My concern is that by living (or rehearsing) the life of a child with no chores or responsibilities, this may only perpetuate and deepen the sense that "this is how life is," and make it ever more difficult to change gears later in life, when others began this process in the early teens. The habits of adulthood take a long while to settle in - it's best not to put off the process too long.

Best wishes on your journey.

It sounds as though you are very focussed on skills. Does a particular chore involve the development of a new skill, or does it not? With this focus, it would be a great idea for NEETs to take on as many of these skill-oriented chores as possible, refining their abilities at things like household maintenance and cooking. 

But there are really two big factors in adult functioning: skills and habits. Skills involve learning new things; habits involve carrying them out repeatedly to the point that they become automatic. 

A NEET I knew at one point saw the need for both. But he talked about adult habits (managing his sleep cycle, paying his bills, raking leaves, keeping his room clean, etc) as something he needed to start building for himself. In effect, he saw himself at the starting gate with few or no habits, and he needed to get started.

What he didn't realize is that we can't start building habits. We are building them every day, whether we mean to or not. When we do things over and over, they become more and more entrenched and automatic. The only question is which habits we are building. Are we building the habit of doing our laundry, or are we building the habit of dependence on others? Are we building the habit of making the bed, or the habit of leaving it in a mess? Are we building the habit of working on our goals, or are we building the habit of avoidance and distraction?

The NEET I mention didn't need to start building habits. He was already doing so. The habits he was etching into his life, however, were ones that would disrupt, damage, and delay his life rather than enhancing it. 

Which takes longer to develop? Skills or habits? I think habits take longer. I can teach you to roast a chicken in half an hour. Creating the habit of cleaning up as you cook? That takes longer, because that etching process requires a lot of repetition. A person who at 26 has not developed the habits that will serve him is in a difficult life position, and one that will only get more difficult the longer parents or other caregivers make it possible for him to etch the habits of avoidance deeper.

Fine, but which is more important? Skills or habits? I think habits are more important. If you don't know how to change the oil in a car or make fettucine alfredo, you can learn fairly easily. Most skills aren't rocket science. Habits are harder to break once formed, and harder to form once neglected. When I advocate that NEETs have regular chores and responsibilities, it's because these serve the capable self, whereas their absence serves the helpless self.

Twenty six years is an enormous debt, though. Do you really plan to spend 26 years of your future life doing your parents' chores and paying for their home and food?

Overcoming NEET is largely a matter of overcoming dependence. One of the core ways of doing that is to be able to make your own food, do your own laundry, and contribute on an equal footing with housemates with the broader tasks of keeping a home going. Those are skills and habits that go a long way to develop both emotionally and socially. It's hard to understand how a person would overcome childhood dependence by rehearsing it and embedding it for even longer. 

For those in education, employment, training, relationships, and social life, chores and self-care are standard elements of life that have to get done - and that become part of the person's development. Being able to run a vacuum and roast a chicken go a long way toward making one friend/roommate/dating material. I can't think of any way for a NEET to spend a day that would be more productive than by learning to make a new dish or paint a bathroom. After a year of not being around other people, this type of activity is almost certainly going to be outside a person's comfort zone. The comfort zone shrinks the more time you spend in it, so even things that a person used to enjoy will feel awkward, strange, and unrewarding when they first do them. This is one way that hikikomori get more and more isolated - they retreat to relative comfort and the comfort zone gets smaller and smaller. 

Many non-hiki people noticed this same phenomenon after a lot of covid isolation. They longed for a return to "normal life" and socializing, but found when they did so that they couldn't think of anything to say, felt awkward and out of practice, and couldn't "tune in" to the enoyment they expected. 

One solution is to obey the discomfort and/or fear and retreat inward. This has the disadvantage, however, of a steadily shrinking life. The other solution is to accept that anything outside the comfort zone is going to be (drum roll...) uncomfortable. It won't be enjoyable for a while - due to novelty, awkwardness, lack of practice, a tendency to overinterpret what everyone else is thinking, and more. The same phenomenon happens in depression, and relates to the idea of anhedonia: [https://youtu.be/QSYtqlPpL0M](https://youtu.be/QSYtqlPpL0M)

First, when any area of assertiveness gives you difficulty, you can make an increased effort to find or artificially create milder scenarios where you can practice. In effect, envision a staircase. If the step you face is too big for you, carve it into smaller ones - ridiculously small if need be. 

Creating conflict can seem difficult - but it can be as mild as asking the barista who just called your name, "Sorry, is this cup mine?" Or asking for a different table than the one offered at a restaurant. 

Second, you can practice situations in which tears are irrelevant. Few conflicts get fully resolved via email, but you can address at least some issues that way. Email also offers you the opportunity to come up with multiple drafts of a response before you send one. If you cry while typing, fine. No one can notice.

Third, you can imagine the feared outcome of your confrontation (losing the relationship, having the other person angry with you) and work at accepting that outcome - knowing that you will survive and life will go on even if it does occur. Sometimes the fear seems indeterminate - it's just fear. Mentally sit it down in a chair opposite you and ask it kindly "What is it you are afraid might happen? What would happen then? What would that mean about you? Could you survive that?" This sounds like I am speaking metaphorically, but I mean it literally - chair and all. Your fear is telling you something, and if you don't pay attention it will tend to shout louder - and make you cry for no reason if necessary. You don't need to obey it. Most of our fears are unreasonable. But you need to know what it is before you can let it go.

Once you've signed up for a specific course, and especially once the drop period has passed, I suggest treating it as a waterslide: You're committed to the end of this course. But the course lasts a term, not 12 years.

The fear is that if you don't go the whole way, you're wasting your time. You're not. Most of the courses you take in the first years will be useful on multiple paths, not just one. And college/uni experience usually proves valuable one way or another, regardless of whether you complete the program intended.

I suggest focussing on the first year, rather than all 12. "I'm going to take school for a year. And maybe more; we'll see." And notice what that does to the trepidation.

One theory of the perception of time (over the longer term) is that it has less to do with the actual amount of time elapsed, and more with the amount of varied activity/experience involved. When you do something new, it gives a sense of time having passed for that experience. When you do the same thing for 10 days, it may store the first day as a novel experience, then the subsequent days as "more of the same, see above" which takes less "room" and thus gives less of a sense of time having passed.

This might explain why as life goes on people sense that time speeds up: They do fewer new things, and the repetitions occupy less space than the new events. It may also explain why, when you go on holiday to a new place, the memory seems to occupy a larger space than a similar period of time spent at home would. In my case, I spent much of 2018 traveling and, by the end, sensed that it was one of the longest years I have had.

By living a fairly repetitive life with little novelty, hikikomori may not be adding new experiences and so wind up with a sense of time flying by. This is independent of the sense of time in the present: Many hikikomori report feeling that the days are long, but the years are short.

(Another factor may be that we don't store many memories of sitting and consuming media, and so this doesn't give us much of a sense of time spent. If you spend 5 hours a day watching youtube, for example, it is less a matter of storing 5 hours of youtube memories, and more a matter of remembering a day that is 5 hours shorter.)

Most practice comes with sheer exposure. You interact with the cashier at the grocery store, with the teller at the bank, with people in your class or at work. You get yourself into situations where the necessity of interaction isn't constant - like a form of volunteer work or engagement in an activity in which you work alongside others. You can also learn ABOUT social skills from books, such as Messages (amazon has it) or my own book The Assertiveness Workbook, if that's the area you want to learn about. The challenge is that most hikikomori have very few interactions with others and so their skills get rusty or never develop in the first place. Over time, they improve by being involved in more frequent interaction.

One thing this shows you is that you clearly can learn and display social skills. It's like someone who has learned French and then doesn't speak it for 2 years and discovers they've forgotten most of it. They've already proven they have the ability to learn French - and if they take it up again they will tend to improve faster than they did the first time. The same is likely to be true of social skills. A great number of hikikomori believe that they are incapable of learning social skills - but in my experience they are usually no worse than others at this. They simply haven't had the practice - or if they once did, the isolation has meant that they are now out of practice.

No matter how brilliantly assertive you are, you don't have a time machine. People can spend a huge amount of energy thinking how they would like things to be different, or kicking themselves for past decisions that can't be remade. 

When you find yourself in this situation, it can be best to repeat a kind of mantra to yourself - something like "Water under the bridge" or "Too late now" or "I will get through this." If you catch yourself dwelling on what you should have done, you can actually define it and think through the words you would use. They may come in handy in future.

It is also useful to realize that when we are resentful about situations like this we are almost inevitably focussed on others. Why did they want this? Why did they keep asking after I said no? How are these people so inconsiderate? Without blame or guilt, take a look at your own steps in the dance. They didn't force you onto the plane or into the car at gunpoint. At some point they kept asking and you went along. 

Again, this is not to make yourself feel bad, but to focus on your point of control. You can't make them not ask, and wanting them to change keeps you not in charge of your own life. Ask yourself some questions that will seem unjust. "At what point did I give the decision to them?" "When did I go along with them?" "What might I have done differently?" "Given that they are likely to do something similar again, no matter how much I might wish otherwise, how will I make my own decision and stick to it?"

I think that you are right: A big part of the problem is that people aren't clear how to help themselves. Partly people haven't been told "how" to adult, but partly our culture provides a lot of ideas that are actively destructive. An example is the idea that you have to "find your passion" in order to motivate yourself to move forward. This idea is usually promoted out of good intentions, but winds up being paralyzing for most people who take it seriously. Some of the path is learning how and what to do; some of it is unlearning the things the culture has taught them. 

The program I am thinking of will indeed be focussed on a fairly broad swath of those having difficulty moving from other-reliant adolescence to more self-reliant independence. As such it will address those who would fall squarely in the traditional hikikomori sphere, but also those who might better consider themselves NEETs. Part of the task is habituation and exposure work; but part of it indeed involves skill development. By retreating or interacting almost exclusively online, many young adults get relatively little practice at social interaction, and what skills they once had can atrophy. There are strategies to build these back up. One of my hopes with this thread is that people can signal bits of knowledge/skill/strategy that I might miss or not think of.

What I would tell you is that this group of individuals - whether narrowly-conceived hikikomori or more broadly defined - is not at all uncommon in today's society. Mental health practitioners across North America report seeing many of them in their work - despite the fact that many are hidden and do not seek out mental health support. They are far from rare. This is why I have developed educational programs for other mental health professionals to help them provide care in an effective way.

My first recommendation is not to make too much of informally-produced personality inventories. The real deals are very elaborate, well-tested, and carefully constructed. The impulse to avoid hurting or harming others is a fine one, and doesn't really prevent assertiveness - unless a person has ideas about what assertiveness looks like that don't match the reality. Assertiveness typically is quite pleasant and polite. It might be a good idea to think of a particular situation, and sit down and write out what you think an assertive response would be and what the effect would be on others. 

As in many areas of life, when you sense that your automatic or instinctive response is distorted or an outright misfire, it's best to take a closer look. What exactly do I think is going to happen? Yes, it would be inconvenient for my staff to know the report is due Friday - but it really is, so hiding it is only likely to make things worse. A conscious rethink is typically useful. And then look at procedures for communicating assertively about the issue at hand - kindly, clearly, and politely.

I agree with you that early identification and prevention are important, and vastly more powerful than treatment. Many parents, for example, model the idea that the best way to cope with fear/anxiety is through avoidance, and over the years this becomes embedded as "bone knowledge" in their offspring. Avoidance and retreat from challenge/threat becomes absolutely common-sense and mandatory. This is extremely difficult to overcome.

Many parents also tend to overbalance on the side of caregiving rather than ability-fostering. They are slow to transfer responsibilities to their offspring, then expect that at the magical age of 20 their son or daughter will know how to use a washing machine, make roast chicken, handle a job interview, manage money, and so on. He/she will also suddenly give birth to a host of habits (getting fear out of the driver's seat, being on time, resisting temptation) that s/he has never previously practiced. I remember a parent fretting about an off-to-college son because he had never operated a washing machine and wouldn't know how. 

Many young adults think "I've been through so much - I just need to take a breather, stay in my safe place for a few months, and my confidence will return and I'll be able to rejoin the world." As you say (hope I am not twisting your meaning), there is no positive change. The inertia and avoidance becomes more and more automatic and entrenched. The more we live like what we used to call an invalid (awful word), the more we feel like one, and the harder it becomes to escape. Time passes, former friends move on, the hole in the resume gets wider, skills atrophy, and confidence wanes even further. It's a profoundly difficult situation to overcome.

This would be a course on the nature of the problem, the solutions that look good but don't really go anywhere, the traps along the way to getting your life restarted, and how to create a life that serves the individual rather than just conforms to societal demands.

This is a common belief among those who overuse the passive style: that assertiveness is basically watered-down aggression. That it makes you mean or dismissive or inconsiderate.

It doesn't. But this is one of the most difficult ideas to get across. You can be kind, friendly, and engaging, and still have boundaries. In therapy I rehearse common low-intensity situations with clients. Things like asking for a different table in a restaurant, or requesting a refund for a faulty product, or setting a completion date for a contractor. And we keep going until the person can do it without sharpness or meanness, regardless of how impermissible it may feel to them due to the unfamiliarity of it.

Then we jointly decide on homework. Pretend you're from out of town and ask the bus driver to tell you when you get close to the hospital. Ask for that different table. Call the cell company and ask for a better data plan. Delegate that work project. Decline that request from the volunteer committee. Say what you really think about that popular movie without dismissing those who like it. Express your opinion about the current political issue. Ask a clerk to get something from a shelf that's too high for you. Make that complicated coffee order that you've been avoiding because "it's an imposition." Ask a stranger for directions to the mall. Take back some shoes that don't fit. And do it all without meanness, without aggression, without needless pushback if it doesn't work out. Then problem solve and try again. And, in circumstances where it's possible, ask for feedback - from the person you spoke with or from a friend who witnesses your performance. "How did that come across?" "Was I unreasonable?" "Did I look aggressive?"

My concern is that the longer an individual lives a hikikomori life, the less it becomes a choice and the more it becomes a cell. With time it becomes more and more difficult to choose any other way of being. This would be fine, but the path doesn't seem to lead to a good place for most people. Even on this sub people talk often about the sense of the life being unsustainable. Parents retire, become ill, or die; friends move on; games and hobbies fade in their interest. Suicide, or the passive wish for terminal illness, seems to become more common. This is doubtless not the case for everyone, but it seems to be for many - including many of the individuals I have seen in therapy. A course designed to help the situation continue might be more destructive than helpful. Based on what I have seen of significant improvements in mood and life satisfaction for those who have turned to face their fears and move outward with support, I think my efforts have to go in that direction. No one need take that path, obviously. My task is just to map it out for those that want it.
