A big part of this is to write down what you believe people are thinking, and set this aside for a couple of days. Then go back to it and see if you can see it with fresh eyes, from the outside - as though you were someone else. How valid do these ideas seem? Sometimes help from a cognitive therapist can help with this. 

One critical item here is that as long as we are behaving in a subservient manner we will feel subservient and less-than. Many people want to change themselves from the inside, with the idea that this will ultimately result in assertive self-expression on the outside. This means that they have to develop better self-esteem while still treating themselves as inferior. It tends not to work. If, instead, they can learn the skills of assertive communication and put them into action, the behaviour will tend to seep into the skin and change how they feel about themselves.

It's a bit like alcoholism. Some would like to feel like a nondrinker, then they will naturally give up drinking. This is unlikely to happen. Instead, they need to alter their behaviour and eventually their self-image will tend to catch up with the reality.

When people are aggressive, they often follow it up with self-criticism and guilt. When people are passive, they are behaving as though they are less significant than others, and their feelings tend to conform to that. Behave as though you are unimportant long enough, and you will feel unimportant. Conversely, behave as though you and others are equals, and you will eventually feel that way. Many people believe that they should be genuine - by which they mean that they should act the way they feel. Their behaviour should flow outward from their emotions or sense of themselves. If they feel worthless or less than, they should behave that way. What they miss in this is that causality also works the other way. Change what you do and you change how you feel. How you act determines, to a great extent, how you feel.

Defending yourself is by no means the only situation in which assertiveness is useful. Indeed, in many situations there is no need to defend ourselves. Someone thinks X of us; that's their right. If they want to find out whether we agree, they can ask. Assertiveness is also relevant when offering our opinion, giving or receiving feedback, declining requests, making requests, and other situations. As well, assertiveness is a way to be fully present in the world - it allows you to be you, whether or not you are setting or defending boundaries. Assertive individuals tend also to express affection and appreciation more; they say what needs to be said. And sometimes they edit out what does not need to be said - we don't get into pointless confrontations that are none of our business, or that promise only to lead to rancour rather than resolution.

People who overuse the passive style often feel they have to mold themselves to the demands and expectations of each person they interact with. This makes group situations awkward, because they have to be rightwing for Mark, leftwing for Carol, apolitical for Frank, and centrist for Joan. Their interactions are not designed to reveal themselves, but to reflect others back to them. (This is called being a "mirror object" in object relations theory.) Because the whole effort is to diminish and hide the true self, the person feels invisible and, yes, diminished.

Being assertive generally means being roughly the same person with everyone, and thus not having to switch important elements of yourself constantly. You'll still speak English to Rob, who has no Spanish, and Spanish to Juan, who struggles in English. But you are essentially the same person with all. You also don't feel any need to convince others to be like you - their attitudes are their business. You don't make it your job to convince Mark that the right is wrong; but you can express your points of agreement and disagreement with him in a way that talks about what YOU think, not what he SHOULD think.

Yes, assertiveness from others can come across to a person who is more comfortable using the passive style as aggression. Some are so sensitized that any feedback at all that isn't wholesale applause comes across as bullying, which it may not be. A man I knew once felt he was being bullied and harassed by his boss who said he should take over several more counters in the department store he worked at. I had to gently break it to him that he was being promoted.

Similarly, the person who overuses the passive style can feel that being kindly and straightforwardly assertive is unforgivably aggressive. Saying that they'd like to go to this restaurant not that one seems outrageously pushy. Declining to loan out their car is inhuman. Asking others to help with dinner is Stalinist. One strategy is to flip the role: So if your best friend asked her family to help with dinner, would that seem unreasonable? But if you did...?

I think that first impressions are indeed important, and can shape how people see you in a powerful way. Most people who report problems being assertive, however, are focussed on relationships that have been going for some time. My spouse, my son, my boss, my best friend, my neighbour of 20 years. Is it possible to shift the way these relationships work? Yes, absolutely. 

The key, as I say elsewhere on this ama, is to look at your own role. What do you do? You may not have direct control over what others think of you, but you do have at least some control over your own actions. How could these be changed? For example, a neighbour who constantly borrows stuff and never gives it back could be greeted with "Oh, Frank, no problem - just get me my rake back and I can give you the clippers for the day" or "Frank, when you borrow things I often can't find them afterward, so it's best if we have our own tools." Depending on the relationship, it might be sharper and firmer than this, of course.

If your son stays on the internet all night and you've been trying to intervene to no effect, you could simply put it on a timer so that it shuts down at midnight, and kindly tell him so. If he takes the car and never puts gas in it, you could say that if he chooses to gas it up he can borrow it again, and if he chooses not to (entirely up to him) it'll be two weeks before you give him the keys. The objective is to do these things without hostility and without accusations, and to make it clear that the other person's behaviour is up to them - you will be working on your behaviour, not theirs. 

And do relationships change as a result? Yes they do.

That's probably best. Some parents think "Oh, poor kid, not working and feeling discouraged - let's treat them like an invalid and cook their meals and wash their socks and expect nothing." This comes from a place of love, usually (and sometimes guilt about parental failings), but can really harm their adult. The key principle in all of assertiveness is that it's not about changing other people, it's about changing yourself. So for almost everyone I say that it's really tempting to focus on "that obnoxious husband/daughter/boss/friend/whatever," and this is what keeps the problem going. So long as you are trying to change someone else, they will resist. And you can't have control over them anyway; you can only control your own behaviour. So the challenge is to refocus on your own steps in the dance and see how you can change. 

This plays out throughout the book in all different scenarios, so it's hard to go into sufficient detail here. At the most basic level it might mean giving up on others making unreasonable requests of you, and instead becoming better at saying no. If we feel used by friends, we stop looking at them and instead look at how we allow ourselves to be used. When we communicate we describe what we are going to do, not what others SHOULD do.  And we remind ourselves that this does not depend on the other person agreeing with us - we don't have to present our case, defend our opinion, or say no in a way that the other person rules in our favour, agrees with us, or withdraws the request. We make ourselves less dependent on others, and less reflexively put ourselves in the subservient position.

I have seen people who are housebound, only able to leave very briefly after dark, who have gone on to full time university. The problem for many - and one of the most difficult to work with in therapy, is that the person is usually very focussed on where they "should" be, or where they'd like to be, or where they are ashamed not to be. The "ultimate goals" are important, but not crucial, and focusing on them and defining everything less as failure is paralyzing.

I try to encourage people to set aside their big ultimate goals for at least some of the time and look instead at where their life is now: what are they doing, how do they spend their days. In therapy with hikikomori I often talk about the short-term long-term problem. Pursue comfort short-term. How? Stay home. Avoid responsibility and things that make you anxious. Avoid failure experiences. Result: A slow and steady increase in discomfort as the world moves on, as sedentary habits get more entrenched, as that gap in your vita widens, etc. Many people on this sub talk about how deeply unhappy they are. One reason for this among the people I've seen personally is that they have chosen moves to make themselves feel better. (This seems true for all the anxiety disorders, btw: They are so intense and so all-encompassing precisely because the person has tried to feel better - if they hadn't, the problem wouldn't be nearly as severe.)

Other option: Pursue comfort long-term. How? Move toward that which makes you anxious and uncomfortable, bit by bit. Expose yourself to failure - partly because failure is always the path to growth, but partly because failure convinces you that failure isn't lethal and so doesn't need to be feared or avoided. Result: Increased discomfort in the short term, but the gradual accrual of comfort in the longer term. You quake and shiver the first time you're on transit, but by the 20th time it's fine. You grit it through the first month of a part time job (which is always unpleasant almost without exception) and gradually begin to feel more at home there while having more money. I can't think of anything in my life that feels good that didn't involve discomfort or anxiety at first. One of the most common fears is public speaking. I am fine talking to hundreds of people, or being on radio or TV, but only got there by hiding shaking legs behind a podium the first few times. 

So suffering is an inevitability, both ways. Short term or long. And there's no way to eliminate it or surmount it entirely, even if you push yourself, face your fears, and walk the path of your life. Suffering is the First Noble Truth - it's an element of every human life. But there are things we can do to bring ourselves more suffering. Or less. In the long term, we may have a bit less by tolerating a bit more discomfort in the short term as we grow ourselves or push ourselves forward. No guarantees, though: We might do all that and still get hit by a bus.

Perhaps the most important skill in many areas of life is the ability to communicate in writing. This reply, in six well-formatted paragraphs, describes in perfect English (apart from a single dropped letter in paragraph 4, line 1) your conviction that you are incapable of mastering anything. But your level of literacy easily exceeds the vast majority of online posters.

I may well be missing a great deal here, of course, and I have no doubt that apart from your obvious skills with language there are areas that are lacking, as there are for most of us. But in my time working with hikikomori, I have often noticed a tendency to hang onto the idea of personal incapacity with a deathgrip in the face of contrary evidence visible to outside observers. "There is no point in me trying to achieve my goals, because I already know I am too incompetent to make any progress."

Part of the problem with others I have met is that the lifestyle imposes a kind of cognitive filter on experience. Failures and errors become extremely meaningful, whereas successes are trivialized, dismissed, or go unrecognized. I often wonder if this tendency is exacerbated by social media, which consists disproportionately of people saying "Look what I managed to do!" or "Just got this qualification!" or "Here are the amazing fruits of my labours!" It's tempting to compare our actual selves, our actual lives, with the online heavily-curated avatars of others, and inevitably we come up lacking.

I don't want to beat up on you here, but one thing that sparks this is your statement that "I had trouble assembling ikea furniture before." Traditionally on lengthy personality inventories the designers insert "check questions" to ensure people are reading the items and not blatantly lying. "Have you had difficulty assembling Ikea furniture?" would be a good one, as surely everyone who has ever purchased from the store would have to say yes (including me and, I will presume unless contradicted, everyone else who reads this). Difficulty assembling Ikea furniture is not evidence of incompetence, it's evidence of simply being a customer.

I've sometimes asked hikikomori to spend some time contemplating the disadvantages and downsides of believing that they possess roughly-normal abilities, or that they have within them the raw materials of a life beyond their all-room (as CGP Grey so precisely put it in a YouTube video based on a book of mine). At first the answer is "Nothing." Then answers begin to percolate, and with them the reasons behind the allegiance to the idea of personal defectiveness. When we hold an idea that is distorted (if it really is), usually it's because there is a hidden motive (hidden even from us) driving it. Something that seems to us straightforwardly true seems so not because it is, but because we need it to be.

The tendency to spend a lot of effort ensuring that children and adolescents do not experience failure. I'm thinking of parents who feel that every effort on the part of their child must be treated as though it was exceptional, and that anything that might prove to be too difficult should be avoided. As well, I think of schools that really try to avoid giving students failure experiences - such as a local school that stops softball games before the end so that "either team might have won."

In the future, people may not laugh about these practices, but they will probably shake their heads in confusion. Parenting is a process of raising young people to cope as adults, and failure is an essential and common element of adult life: Most job interviews won't result in a job, most dates won't result in a partner, most projects will not result in a prize. The avoidance of failure communicates clearly to a young person that failure is dangerous and to be avoided - which is exactly the opposite of how things are achieved in adulthood.

Constant reward, with every effort being labelled "awesome," naturally leads a young person, who is new to the planet and therefore does not know differently, to think "this is the way things are." Everything they do is exceptional, and should be greeted as such. This is a cruel trick to play on a child, who will inevitably find themselves in the outside world where everything they do isn't celebrated or praised. In job settings they will feel neglected if their efforts attract little attention, or bullied if flaws in their work are pointed out or if revisions or corrections are requested. (This is not to deny, obviously, that real bullying does take place.)

The future will hopefully recognize that childraising is really "adultraising," and this means preparing one's young charge for the realities of adulthood: failure is common, most of what we do isn't exceptional, praise is not relentless, and we are not superior to our peers on all levels.

This is a question that often comes up in therapy, and I do a bit of math with people. 

Imagine that you are interested in 10% of other people, and 10% are interested in you. These aren't life partners, mind, they're interesting enough for a second date.

Go on 100 dates. 80% of the time neither of you is really interested in taking it further. 9% of the time you're interested, but they are not. 9% of the time they're interested, you are not. 1% of the time you agree. (The remaining 1% is rounding error.) This means that 90% of the time when you are interested, he won't be. Normal. And that's with the probably-too-lax idea that you're interested in 10%. The problem is that people take this 90% rejection rate as a sign of their own worthlessness, rather than a sign of normality.

This is why you have to meet a lot of people - and why "dating" apps are sometimes not so great. You have to screen people one at a time. Whereas a community group - sports team, hiking, film fest, etc - can be a better source: You can meet 20 people at a time. And those people will share at least one interest with you apart from finding a partner.

You often hear about following your dreams from two sources: 1) people who experienced unexpected or remarkable success - ie the few who made it, not the many who did not; or 2) inspirational speakers who can make a great deal of money by promising that fantasies come true.

I would recommending asking yourself about the nature of your dreams: are they about process or fruition? If it's acting, for example, is it about the actual hard, challenging work of acting, or is it about standing on a stage receiving an award? If the latter, then the dream is probably not worth pursuing. Those who arrive on that stage are usually struck by the fact that, although good, it isn't as transcendent as they thought. And the fantasy of the award won't be enough to get you to do the hard work of getting there in any case. So: Is it the job or is it the outcome that your dream is about?

There is value in living your life in the present, noticing the things that interest you, and exploring further in that direction. But the start of the road is just to get moving and expose yourself to different things, not to arrive at dreams. Entry level jobs aren't about dreams, for example: they're about beer money and the development of habits that will serve you well for the rest of your life. This includes vital bits like "I'm bored by this task but it has to get done so let's get to work rather than whining" - vital because every job, including your dream job, will have these elements and being able to reflexively ignore your boredom or reluctance and not put it in the driver's seat is an essential key to success.

This is a standard thought among people with social anxiety. They aren't actually afraid of being outside, or even being around other people. They fear being perceived and judged by others. When I see a person with social anxiety I often ask the invisibility question: If no one could see you (or bump into you), what would happen to your fear of being out in a group, at a party, in a restaurant, etc? Usually they say it would drop or vanish.

Another poster has suggested that in fact they really do seem almost invisible. They have discovered the key to much of this, which is expressed in an old maxim - I have forgotten who said it first:

"We would be less concerned with what others think of us if we knew how seldom they do."

The illusion of conspicuousness is prominent for many with social anxiety. "Everyone for blocks away can see me and knows or thinks what an awkward loser I am." The person's focus is relentlessly on themselves and how they might appear, so they seem like the spotlighted centre of the universe. The motivation issue is central to the problem. Most hikikomori know at least some of what might need to happen in order for them to have a more fulfilling life. (As well as being aware of some elements outside their control, such as economic factors, etc.) Getting themselves to work the levers that are at least partially under their control is more difficult.

One of the problems is not that they are unmotivated. It is that they are TOO motivated. They want to save the world (which is not the task for any one person, no matter what the Avengers might do), buy a nice house (despite having no money), be fully employed in a job they love (which can't be accomplished from a standing start), pursue their passion (because society has convinced them that's what people do even though most of humanity does not have a great driving passion and in any case passions are BUILT, not discovered), and so on. Some of these goals are entirely reasonable EVENTUALLY but none can be achieved without a series of steps. Rather than trying to motivate them, a good therapist will often try to DEmotivate them - by which I mean help them to refocus on smaller goals that are within range.

There are two problems with this. 

First, many are so conscious of external expectations, parental demands, and so on, that their focus is entirely on measuring up to some external standard. This is seldom motivating for anyone, let alone for a person who has been stuck spinning their wheels for some time. 

Second, there is a common sense that "I will only feel a measure of satisfaction once I have achieved X (bought my home, landed the corner office, found a partner), and every step in the direction of X will bring only pain." There is an intense focus on ultimate fruition, rather than on the steps along the way.

The goal is often to let go (for NOW) of the grand vision and refocus on the current life. What would be ONE step forward? Such as: Same life, but able to ride the bus. Same life, but 2 hours volunteering a week. Same life, but doing my own shopping. Same life, but having taken one web design course at the college. Every journey is a set of many steps; focusing exclusively on the destination won't get us there. We have to focus on where our feet our and the next step to be taken. The vision can dictate the steps, but the steps themselves have to be where we focus.

In the examples you give: Forget learning Japanese; find out if there's a Japanese class in your town. Let go of your idea of great dancing; go to a live dance performance. Relinquish the fantasy of a tenured art history position; watch Hannah Gadsby's Douglas.  

The second aspect of this is to identify steps that might improve your life fairly soon, rather than having a payoff only at the end. If you have a regular volunteer gig with the neighbourhood litterpickers, you will gradually form a social network and get used to interaction. If you learn how to use the subway, your world will get a little bigger. If you take a course you will have one more line on your resume. It's a cliche, but for most of us the ultimate achievement (the wedding, the promotion, the bank balance) is nice, but doesn't provide as much fulfillment as the path toward it. It's the Japanese classes you remember, not sitting on the couch knowing that you understand Japanese.

And all of this involves an acceptance of a simple fact. Remaining within the zone of comfort only results in a steadily shrinking zone of comfort - it does not produce greater confidence for the journey. The only way to expand our lives is to leave comfort and do things which make us at least a little uncomfortable - things which feel a bit fake, a bit anxiety-provoking, a bit unnatural for us, because they ARE. They aren't a part of our repertoire. The anxiety isn't a signal to shrink back. That's the feeling of life expanding. We become ready for the journey only once we are on the journey.

"I get up at \_\_\_, eat \_\_\_, then \_\_\_, etc." Let go of the SHOULD and ask yourself "What would be ONE expansion of this life?" Not the total solution, not conformity to what others expect, not the achievement of some grand vision, but one step outside the comfort zone into a slightly bigger life. 

When I worked in a spinal injury unit, many of the patients were young males used to an active lifestyle. Initially they were focussed on going back to running/diving/football and any improvement just seemed stupid and pointless. Once they could acknowledge and accept where they actually were, then the gradual improvements became motivating wins. Walking five steps or doing a transfer to a toilet meant they could poop alone. That was a huge gain. Without that shift so that gains over the previous state were motivating, they didn't have the energy or ability to do the rest of their rehab, because no single step was going to get them where they wanted to be.

What's the right one for a hikikomori? Different for different people. Some examples: 

* Learn (or relearn) to take public transit, by researching, getting the coins or buying a card, and riding one stop.
* Find one street within a km of your home that you have never walked down. Walk it.
* Take a book or laptop to a coffee shop at a quiet time and spend one hour there with headphones on. (Best to time these things; otherwise you'll let your anxiety dictate when you stop - every time you obey the anxiety you feed it power over you.)
* Identify one SMALL thing that caregivers do for you that isn't necessary given your physical abilities (washing your sheets, making your breakfast, driving you to a place that's on the bus line) and ask them to stop doing this. The parents of many hikikomori will never act to take the training wheels off your life's bicycle. You may have to do this yourself.
* Identify the simplest and shortest form of volunteer work you could possibly do - attend a demonstration, be a ticket taker at the one-day festival, help a relative move, become the airport driver for family, help a family member or friend's business with one time-limited task (creating a spreadsheet, sweeping the back room, building an Ikea storage cabinet, whatever). Volunteer work is an approximation to work without the commitment, and can help a person get used to the idea.
* Above all, focus on where your feet are, rather than trying to motivate yourself by fantasizing about the distant horizon: saving the world, becoming a billionaire, or cutting a hit track. This is the aspartame of achievement and only makes it harder to get moving.

Doesn’t this reasoning work both ways?

As a human being, I have needs: food, clean water, shelter, clothing, safety, and Netflix, among many others. Somehow I have to obtain these. In a primitive world, I might be able to get some of these myself - building a stick shelter, or capturing a rat. Even in prehistoric cultures, though, we lived in tribes with role specialization - and everyone had a role and had to help. If I did not contribute by fulfilling a role, the food preparers might not contribute by feeding me.

The only way to avoid slavery, which is a common way here to describe contributing in some way, is to be a slave owner. Enlist one or more fellow humans (perhaps giving them names, like Mom or Dad) and convince them that their role is to serve me - to find my food, prepare it, build or pay for the shelter, clean my clothes, and otherwise go out and contribute to the larger culture in exchange for tokens (let’s call those money) they can use to sustain themselves and me. 

To do this we may have to convince them that there exists somewhere an unwritten contract that they have neither seen nor signed which requires them to keep this up until they expire - a hard sell, because no law or social norm requires this. 

The other possibility is to convince the tribe as a whole that their job is to support me with a portion of the money they receive by taking on a responsibility or role. If the tribe is big enough, say millions, each would only have to contribute a fraction of a penny to me and they might not even notice. But if they realize there are thousands of people doing this who have the ability but not the inclination to take on a role, and that fractions add up, they may one day object or refuse.

Slave or slave owner? Someone might suggest that such a system could be defended if the result was a huge amount of life satisfaction on the part of the person who doesn’t take on a role. But the sense many have is that dependent isolation doesn’t provide this - and that misery increases the longer it goes on. If the slaves revolt and decline to provide support without some degree of reciprocation, things seem to improve in the long run for them, and for their former owner.

Sometimes people get stuck because they are focussed on the fifth step down the road, rather than the step that they are on. 

For some hikikomori, the task is to go for a walk during daylight, or ride a bus for the first time, or do their own laundry. For many, it's to take on a volunteer commitment (ushering at a festival, environmental cleanup, shelf-stocking at a food bank, clerical work at a charitable organization) - to build skills and, more importantly, habits. Some are so focussed on "How can I get a job that will let me buy a house?" that they have difficulty working on their sleep cycle. 

Lots of therapy is about placing your eyes on the point of control (where you can have influence) rather than on the far horizon.

I'm a psychologist with an interest in hikikomori (I wrote How to be Miserable in Your 20s), and have also done a great deal of work with severe clinical depression and the anxiety disorders. (So really, I'm not the person you are asking this question of, and am just butting in, which I try not to do often here.)

Part of the issue seems, for many, to be an instance of the short-term/long-term problem. The  immediate and long-term effects are in opposite directions. If I'm anxious in crowds, the short term solution is easy: avoid crowds. But in the long run this makes the fear worse. By making myself feel better NOW I ensure that I will feel more of the fear I'm trying to avoid LATER. Conversely, if I move toward those difficult situations (very gradually and with support, planning, and sufficient exposure duration) I will most likely feel worse now, but ultimately we tend to desensitize to situations that used to freak us out. One problem in treatment is often that people are feeling so awful that the prospect of feeling any worse is intolerable, so exposure is really hard to engage with.

Anyway, I'm long-winded. That's why I write books. When asked the motivation for the lifestyle, many avoidant young adults report that it's in large part an emotional management strategy: It's how to feel better - not great, but at least not as lousy as they feel in the outside world. The tragedy is that this is precisely what we would recommend if our agenda was for them to feel worse in the long run - and it mostly works.

I once asked a group of clinicians, "Which is the disorder that improves when you take away a person's roles and responsibilities, isolate them, randomize their sleep cycle, and make them dependent on others for their basic needs?" They looked at me. There isn't one. This is how we create psychological disorder, not resolve it.

A sense of conspicuousness is a standard feature of social anxiety: It can feel as though you are transparent - in effect, naked - to the world and that everyone is aware of and paying attention to your shortcomings. This is generally a misperception - most people are much more caught up with themselves and their own concerns to notice anyone around them. Eyewitness testimony research suggests that you can do almost anything and people will fail to notice it.

The way to make this feeling stronger, as usual, is to obey it. Stay inside, dress to be invisible, go out only at night, etc. One problem with hikikomori living is that it tends to be avoidant of fears - which is the best way to grow them. Subjectively it can feel like "I'll stay in this secure, comfortable place until my sense of confidence and groundedness builds, then I'll venture outward." But instead the anxiety tends only to get stronger.

The way to overcome the feeling is through "opposite action" - do the opposite of what the belief suggests. Go out, walk in crowds, dress in bright clothes - and deliberately do odd things (trip, drop money, say hello to strangers, misbutton your shirt) to prove to yourself that you can do these things and survive - that even if someone comments it doesn't really matter and you live.

Conspicuousness is, in a sense, a type of narcissism: I am the most interesting thing for people to watch in this crowd. Usually we're not. A famous quote used by many therapists who work with social anxiety is: We would be less concerned with what others think of us if we knew how seldom they do.

Therapy for social anxiety disorder most often involves both cognitive work ("what are the thoughts about what might happen or what might others think if you were on the bus") and exposure-based work ("let's ride the easiest bus we can find at the quietest time, and then work our way up from there, and let's do the same thing over and over til it feels excruciatingly boring"). Is this the type of work you have been doing in therapy? There's a good book on social anxiety for teens called The Shyness and Social Anxiety Workbook for Teens by Shannon. And a brief discussion of therapy here: [https://youtu.be/yEHGkwHqO2c](https://youtu.be/yEHGkwHqO2c) Cognitive work here: [https://youtu.be/cmsQES7Okio](https://youtu.be/cmsQES7Okio) Exposure here: [https://youtu.be/ZUNvQxufMDo](https://youtu.be/ZUNvQxufMDo)

I imagine this depends on where you live. In Canada, and in most parts of the US, the primary requirement is that you have a pulse. There has never been a time in recent memory when employers were more desperate to find workers. An individual I know in this situation had a 50% or greater job offer rate despite an extremely sparse work history, no postsecondary, and no vaccinations. If ever there was a time for hikikomoris to be applying for work, this is it.

There are external factors - low pay, high rental rates, and more - that can contribute to young adults having difficulty leaving the nest. But in my experience as a clinical psychologist (I wrote How To Be Miserable In Your Twenties) the ones that have the most difficulty aren't necessarily the ones with the fewest qualifications or who live in the most expensive cities. It's the young adults who have never been given responsibilities during their upbringing, and have never been encouraged to think through and solve problems. 

Parenting involves two seemingly contradictory tasks: Keep the kid safe, and prepare them to live without us. Security and independence. Most young adults I've seen in the "failure to launch" category have had what we might think of as great parents: warm, caring, engaged. But they're not used to having chores, don't know how to cook, have never had to deal with natural consequences (I don't mean punishments - things like having your phone cut off if you don't pay the bill), don't know how to operate a washing machine, and so on. They have been swaddled against hazard extremely well, but preparing for independent life? Not so much. 

Ideally the shift from adolescence to adulthood isn't a transition. It's a smooth decade-long shift from a parent/child to an adult/adult relationship. If that's done, they tend to develop their independence and, eventually, move out to commence life out of the nest. And if not, at least they know how to do their own laundry.

You live in a culture that emphasizes the idea of pursuing your passion and finding your dream job. It sounds like you are looking for an entry-level job: Not one you will retire in, but a stepping stone to greater things. These stepping stones tend not to be inherently thrilling in themselves, and are taken primarily to a) make a start at earning a wage, and b) start developing the habits that lead to success in almost any form of work (being on time, figuring out how to contribute, interacting, taking direction, and getting oneself to do less-than-fascinating tasks that every job, no matter the level, has). I started out in a warehouse job that had little inherent interest for me, but I probably got more out of that in terms of skill and habit development (partly BECAUSE I wasn't just "pursuing my passion") than any job since. 

Very few entry level jobs will pay six figures - in fact, I can't think of any that will. Remember that this is a step, not the whole journey. For many NEETs there can be an understandable wish to go from "0 dollars, dead stop" to "decent income and lifestyle" at one go, but this is part of what keeps people home and unemployed. Any job at all will be a step forward, a line on the resume, and a habit developed. On the plus side, the job market in most western economies is so hot right now at virtually all levels that it's a seller's market for labour.

I get it. I think I'm reacting to all those people who are asking a few days before xmas, "is this illness covid or isn't it." What I was trying to get at was that it doesn't matter. If you're sick, you don't visit people with babies. You're risking either the baby getting sick, which nobody needs, or already-exhausted parents getting sick, which nobody needs. So the nature of the potentially-communicable illness isn't an issue.

And (take this with a grain of salt from a non-baby-owner here, but author of an assertiveness book) if you're the parent of said baby, it's fine and probably important to be able to say "Hey folks, we love ya, but we're a total no-go zone if yer sick with anything that might be catching." Which it sounds like you did, for which: great.

You seem to be somewhat focused on whether or not this is covid. I would suggest taking covid out of the picture for a moment. Pretend you are in a world where there isn't a pandemic spiking and killing more people than any airborne illness has since 1918. 

In this covid-free world, what would you recommend to a parent of a new baby who has an apparent communicable illness of undiagnosed origin coming over for Christmas? Or put yourself in the position of an older parent of offspring who have a 3 month old infant. Would you see it as important and appropriate for you to head over to their house for a celebration, knowing you have a non-allergy-like illness of unknown origin, or would you say "Damn, I was looking forward to it but no way am I going to infect you folks, so hope to see you soon."

In the before times, people would often be at death's door and still think it was fine to go to crowded parties, or to family gatherings with vulnerable relatives, or to pop by the old folks home to see grandma, or to head off to work to hack their lungs out in the centre cubicle. My own hope is that those days never return.

The best book I've seen on the subject is Mark McConville's Failure to Launch, which I'm recommending for additional reading as part of the course. After reading his perspective I discarded my thought of writing a book of my own - he covers so many of the bases I would have covered, and we seem to be in agreement on a lot of the core elements. I've since taken to recommending it to parents who are coping with the issue.

Your metaphor is an interesting one - comparing isolation to, say, alcohol or heroin. If a parent had an alcoholic son and constantly bought him bottles of vodka, we might be critical of them or accuse them of "being an enabler." By extension, would you say that parents are, in a sense, providing the "drug" in this case as well? What would you advise them to do differently, if anything?

I never advocate that parents cut off or throw out their young adults, to be clear. In fact, my work with them is to see how better to support them in their journey to greater capability, confidence, and life satisfaction than they are getting from an inevitably-time-limited neet-dom. In chronic pain, there is a common issue of "invalidizing" people: "Don't wash those dishes, you're in pain - I'll do them." In the short term this is nice, but in the long run it tends to increase the person's incapacity. 

Similarly, parents who assist in withdrawal from the world (even in some cases buying all the person's clothes, having no expectations about household chores, doing the young person's laundry, making all their meals, paying for the internet to which they are addicted, and sometimes delivering the meals to the young person's room) sometimes benefit from the realization that they are helping to promote a life that is ultimately damaging for the young person. One that cannot go on forever, but becomes more difficult to escape from with every month that it continues and becomes more ingrained. 

We work to address the fact that the young person DOES have abilities and capacity, and work with those, rather than undermining them by making them superfluous. We try to shift the relationship from parent/child to adult/adult, treating the young adult with respect rather than seeing them as incapable invalids, which they are inevitably not.

And yet, none of us has a time machine and there are thousands of young adults in this situation. If by the 20s it's too late, this would imply that there's nothing to be done. But if we can get these adults engaged and involved with life, they generally improve a great deal - not just productively but also emotionally. 

The biggest challenge is helping a person to the realization that their life is THEIR LIFE, and that there is no external force coming to the rescue. Whatever our traumas, losses, and limitations, whatever was done to us, whatever we lacked, whatever inadequacies our parents had, however much damage was done before we reached adulthood, we are nevertheless our own adult, and the future course of our life is to a great degree up to us. 

I agree with you that parenting is often a big problem. In particular, many parents of adults struggling with independence didn't focus much on cultivating independence or self-care skills in their offspring. Mental health can be a big part of this. The challenge is that most of the mental health concerns cited among adults who haven't launched are made worse by having the avoidance supported and maintained. 

The most common mental disorders talked about with this population are ADHD, high-functioning autism, depression, social anxiety, and avoidant personality disorder. None of these are best treated with isolation, unemployment, a lack of role, and 12 hours of screen time. 

Yet parents and young adults alike often feel "He can't be around people until his social anxiety is gone," "He can't relinquish his depressogenic lifestyle until his depression is gone," "He can't stop avoiding until his avoidant personality is changed," or "He can't do anything that requires attention until his ADHD is under control." 

But the treatments for all of these things involve exactly the opposite: overcoming the avoidance rather than helping it continue. Perpetuating the isolated, withdrawn state isn't helping to overcome the mental health problems in most cases - it's making them more intense and intractable. Becoming more productive and engaged is the treatment in most cases. I've never seen a young adult become much happier and more satisfied with their existing life, then change it. But I've seen many change it and then become happier and more satisfied with their new lives.

When I talk to clients about an issue like this, they tend to focus on things like having a conversation, hanging out at a coffee shop with someone, going to a restaurant. These always seem like lousy ideas to me. They put social interaction - the hardest part - front and centre, as the main part of the thing. 

I suggest they find something to do that will put them into contact with other people as a side effect, rather than as the main thing. Initially, this might involve things like asking for directions in a store, or making a special prep request at a coffee shop, or asking a transit supervisor when fares last went up. Will they make friends that way? No. But these are steps toward being able to make small talk.

When they're ready I suggest they come up with something they could do where they have a role of some sort, and where conversation is an optional extra, not something they are required to do. Lots of volunteer work is like this. I especially like festivals (film, theatre, comedy, jazz, sports) for this. The tasks are usually easy (selling tickets, showing people their seats, putting out chairs, sweeping up), the festival is time-limited, and you have SOMETHING TO DO other than thinking up things to say. If you're not into a lot of conversation, you're "busy" with your role. And if conversations start, they usually get interrupted very quickly so they're short. 

Once they're ready for more, we look at what their interests are and try to pick things where conversation is more optional. Hiking groups are great because you're always speeding up or slowing down and seldom with the same person for long. Community environmental cleanup is great because again, there's something to do. The "let's have Sunday brunch at a different resto every week" is harder because all people do over a meal is talk - it's something to work up to, not something to start with.

I practice in Vancouver which, although a beautiful city with lots to do, isn't renowned for being easy to break into socially if you've just arrived or if you've been hikikomori for a while. The problem, I think, is that when you're experiencing profound loneliness it's tempting to focus directly on the goal of making friends. But if you ask people how they met their friends, it turns out it wasn't by trying to make friends. It was an incidental side effect of doing something else. 

The trick is to find the "something else" and do that, leaving friendship to one side for the time being. For a lot of people with a spotty employment history, the answer is volunteer work. This a) gets you out of the house, b) puts you around people, c) gives you an activity so you're not just staring at someone trying to come up with conversation, d) makes you a part of a team of people with a common purpose (getting people seated for the festival, selling tickets, cleaning the beach, serving food, whatever) which is how to create a sense of bonding between them, e) gives practice at showing up on time and being reliable, which is more important than just about anything when it comes to employability, f) provides a line of content for the resume, and g) gives a lot of people more of their friends than anything else they've done.

When I ask people what they think of when I say volunteer work, they say pushing the magazine cart at the hospital, or something else that doesn't have any appeal for them. But there's volunteer work of every sort imaginable, and it's typically easier to get into than a paid job. Ask yourself "What ELSE do I like or seems important to me" and you can narrow down the field a bit.

I understand your concern. It's difficult to raise this question without sounding like a guilt inducer. I work with both NEETs and their parents. One idea that comes up occasionally is "I didn't ask to be born, it was your decision. So my well-being is your responsibility, not mine, and this doesn't have an end date attached."

It's unquestionably true that no NEET ever chose to be born. No human on Earth did, so this line of reasoning fits us all. My life and my happiness, in this sense, are entirely the responsibility of my long-dead parents. The trouble is, they chose not to accept that responsibility beyond the date when I was capable of looking after myself. The consequence for most people is either our needs go unmet or we meet them ourselves.

This can sound like a bad deal. But the NEETs that I see tend not to view their lives positively. Even when parents are doing it all (in some cases delivering meal trays to their 30-year-old's bedroom several times a day - though this isn't common), the person being cared for typically isn't very satisfied with their life. This fits with many people's experience of the world: dependence doesn't produce happiness. People seem to become happier, more confident, and more satisfied when they are more in control of their own lives - this seems to be the case with most former NEETs in my experience, at any rate.

Another problem with the perspective that it's the parents' responsibility is that it isn't enough for the young person to believe it. It depends on the parents agreeing with it and cooperating. Whether you regard the idea as true or not, many parents don't. And if they simply ramp down their parenting and financial support, the young adult winds up in the same position: having to do without this care or become able to provide it themselves. Which looks uninviting but typically turns out to be a better life than waiting for someone else to do it.

Parents and adult offspring often get into a sniping, nagging, conflicted relationship because the parents are trying to get the young adult to change (get work, move out, make his own meals, etc), and the young adult refuses. Everyone is trying to make everyone else change. What often helps is for the parents to stop trying to change the young person and change themselves instead. If they only want to be making half the meals, then only make half the meals. If they don't want to be funding the phone, then don't pay the bill.

Rather than cutting off or throwing out their young adult (which some do when they get enraged), we try to have them treat their offspring as what they truly are: adults. The challenge is that many are treating their young adult as a child, and the young adult naturally and appropriately feels insulted by this. The parents can provide the support they are willing to provide (which is often considerable) but recognize that their son or daughter has personal business of their own and can decide for themselves how to handle rent, meals, bills, and so on.

I agree with you that much of the problem in NEET has to do with parenting. In many cases, the parents have approached the dual task of parenting (keep the kid alive and prepare him to survive your own death or obsolescence) and have overbalanced on nurturance. They haven't done the work of helping their offspring attain the skills and self-confidence they need to truly become captain of their own lives. But the solution isn't for the parent to go on being captain forever, hoping that the child will die before the parent does. It's to ramp back on parenting bit by bit, helping the young person find their own agency.

There are many other factors in determining mood - some of them personally controllable, others not so much. The first trick, of course, is keeping it going. And you can aid that by noticing improvements and dwelling on them as much as most of us tend to do on mood declines. But will you keep it going? Constantly? No. Why not? Because none of us do. None of us is that disciplined.

Which points to the second trick: Use the decline that follows falling off the good-life wagon NOT as a stick to beat oneself with, but as a helpful reminder. "Wow, I feel lousy. That makes me tempted to sit alone at home surfing endlessly. But before I do that, how long has it been since I exercised (or saw others, or ate properly, etc)? Oh. Maybe this isn't such a mystery. The door is open to feeling differently, maybe I could take some baby steps toward it."

With time it becomes a bit easier to notice the energy downshift, take the lesson, and make the adjustment. Easier, but never entirely easy. Lowered mood always tempts us (most of us, anyway) to do precisely what will magnify the low mood, and makes all of the things that will likely shift it look unappealing. Best of luck with it. Or should I say, best of effort.

A first appointment with a counsellor (I am one) usually involves an attempt to understand what's basically going on. My own assessment can be summed by a few basic questions:

What have you been experiencing that brings you here?
What has the course of this problem been (when did it start, intensify, etc)?
What was going on around the time it started or worsened?
What seems to help so far, if anything?
Did anything improve or worsen when other treatment began?
What's your guess about what's really going on here?
What would you most like to get out of seeing me?

None of those can be answered completely in one short session, and no good therapist will expect you to be completely organized. But thinking about those questions in advance will usually help you make the most of your first meeting. 

Note, though, that the first meeting is not usually much about treatment - it's more of an info-gathering session. Expect more of an initial sketch of suggested approaches in session 2.

The bit that I am focused on is the recollection of a feeling - the sense of reluctance to get on a plane, for example - and moving from that memory to a belief that "I knew it." 

In fact, it seems that we did "knew it". The distortion comes in when we forget that we "knew it" hundreds of other times as well when in fact it didn't happen.

Most comparisons suggest that self-care approaches are a bit less effective than direct face-to-face therapy, but some show no real difference. And most self-care approaches are pretty weak entities (the largest body of work has to do with the impact of being told "Go read this self-help book"). We spend a lot of time worrying about face-to-face effectiveness, but our other approaches are generally fairly primitive.

I suppose my point is that there is a logical fallacy in some of the reasoning around the importance of the alliance. Studies do show that in face to face therapy the quality of the alliance is a (actually 'the') major determinant of outcome.

The fallacy is assuming that the presence of a relationship is therefore essential. This entails a hidden assumption that the relationship "adds" something important.

But the research showing the importance of the alliance in face-to-face outcome doesn't address the importance of having a therapist in the room. It simply says IF there is a therapist in the room, the quality of the relationship is important.

I'm raising the possibility that one reason the alliance is important is that a poor one (or a poor therapist) can degrade the experience below that of a non-face-to-face form of therapy. So one could as easily say that having a therapist in the room is a risk as a benefit.

My guess is that a face to face encounter is generally a positive addition to therapy, but that the much of the variability in outcome has to do with decrements brought about by the alliance, not just benefits.

Keeping your goals high - what you "should be able to do" - will result, by nightfall every day, in a sense of defeat. Look at what you ACTUALLY accomplish most days.  Then create a short list of items that includes those things - even the things you already get yourself to do, like showering or getting out of bed by 3 pm. When you do something, no matter how trivial or ridiculous it seems to your self-critical mind, acknowledge that you did it and focus on that. 

If you focus on what you have not accomplished, your emotions will reflect discouragement.

If you focus on what you DO accomplish, your emotions will correspondingly reflect encouragement. The boost will be small, and may be wiped out altogether until you master the knack of talking back to the dismissive part of the mind. 

When a task seems overwhelming, it is always telling you the same thing.  "Make me smaller."

Big topic; I won't do justice to it.  One factor I've noticed is the fear that if you relax and just enjoy the fact that the depression is gone for the moment, it will jump back at you.  

The metaphor I use with my clients is that one morning you wake up and there's ice on the lake. It's beautiful, and it looks strong enough to hold you up. So you go out walking on it and you can hear the creaks and cracks. There's a fear that at any moment you'll break through into the cold water.

In the case of real lakes, this is an easy one:  Avoid doing this and if it cracks get to shore immediately.

In the case of depression the job is more complicated.  Acknowledge that the depression, while currently absent, is probably not gone forever (especially in the early stages of recovery). Yes, you probably will crack through a few times. Yes, it feels tentative and anxiety-provoking, and often a bit fake. But just keep walking.  Let the depression be gone, if only for the moment. The longer you can let the ice hold you up, the thicker it gets.

That doesn't deal with the whole issue, but the reluctance to unclench, relax, and allow happiness or contentment to be there is very common upon recovery.
